A co-production by Centre d’Art Contemporain Genève and Kamel Lazaar Foundation.

Exhibition view of the Biennale de l’Image en Mouvement 2026, Becoming the Ocean, at Quechlet El Attarine in Tunis, as part of the 8th edition of Jaou Tunis.

Photos: @mehdi.ben.temessek

Hajra Waheed 
A River Runs Beneath, 2026 
single-channel video installation, 14’48” 

A River Runs Beneath follows a village chief of a fishing community as he travels at night from the river towards the sea. Shot in one seemingly continuous take and unfolding in real time, the film follows his passage through darkness, guided by his own refrain. 

For generations, fishing communities have lived along these waters, with knowledge passed through direct transmission: observation, repetition, and embodied practice. 

The body is inseparable from the land, and from waters increasingly shaped by struggles over livelihood and access. To move through them is to carry memory into an uncertain present. 

The film’s slowness becomes a refusal of disappearance and acceleration. Time breaks to the rhythm of a low hum and the act of navigation. 

To remain with this passage is to remain with a place under pressure, and with what it carries. There is no resolution, only duration. A quiet insistence against erasure.

A look back at My home is.., a zine-making workshop led by Molka Braiek at B7L9 Art Centre.

Through personal memories, emotions and creative expression, participants explored what home means to each of us and how the places we belong to shape our stories.

A space to remember, create and share.

__

لمحة من ورشة «بيتي هو..»، ورشة صناعة مجلّة فنية بإشراف ملكة بريك، في مركز الفنون B7L9.

من خلال الذكريات الشخصية والمشاعر والتعبير الإبداعي، اكتشف المشاركون معنى البيت بالنسبة لكلّ واحد منهم، وكيف تساهم الأماكن التي نشعر بالانتماء إليها في تشكيل قصصنا.

مساحة للتذكّر والإبداع وتبادل الحكايات.

The opening of BIM'26 in Tunis on October 24 continued at the Bir Lahjar Cultural Center with performances by Trân Tran⁠, rita elhajj⁠, and Orfeo Aurora Lili - なごり⁠— intimate and powerful moments that resonated with the works of the Biennale.⁠
⁠
Before Tunis, these performances were first presented in Geneva during the opening of FAAB B collective’s exhibition “Ce qui dérive résiste encore” at L’Arcade — Centre d'Art Contemporain Genève.⁠
⁠
The performances and the exhibition reflect the FAAB G collective’s (Acronym in French for Asian Anti-Racist Feminists Based in Geneva) desire to challenge the dominant narratives that have contributed to rendering certain histories, identities, and memories invisible, marginalized, or oversimplified, while restoring the presence of those long excluded from official representations.⁠
⁠
•⁠
⁠
Le vernissage de la BIM'26 à Tunis s'est prolongé au Centre Culturel Bir Lahjar avec les performances de Trân Tran⁠, rita elhajj⁠ et Orfeo Aurora Lili - なごり⁠, des instants intimes et puissants qui ont résonné avec les œuvres de la Biennale.⁠
⁠
Avant Tunis, elles ont été présentées en premier lieu à Genève lors du vernissage de l'exposition du collectif FAAB B « Ce qui dérive résiste encore » à L'Arcade du Centre d'Art Contemporain Genève.⁠
⁠
Les performances et l'exposition traduisent la volonté du collectif FAAB G (Féministes Antiracistes Asiatiques Basé.e.x.s à Genève) d’interroger les récits dominants qui ont contribué à invisibiliser, marginaliser ou simplifier certaines histoires, identités et mémoires, tout en restituant des présences longtemps tenues à l’écart des représentations officielles.⁠
⁠

Lara Tabet 

Marseille Overflow, Les Catalans, 2022 

Toxicity and aquatic violence usually unseen beneath the water’s surface are rendered visible. 

As part of Lara Tabet’s artistic-scientific practice oscillating between microscopic and macroscopic scales, these works stem from her research questioning the anthropocentric readings of aquatic ecologies. 

In Marseille Overflow, contaminated Mediterranean waters in Marseille are sampled following an urban sewage spill to be reincubated onto gelatin photographic film, and Nitrate spotlights damaged nitrate negatives digitized by the artist due to their chemically toxic and highly unstable nature. In both instances, the agency of biochemical matter reveals the images, highlighting the autonomous performativity of micro-organisms – notably when experiencing displacement.

Imane Djamil 

Slow Days in the Fortunate Isle, 2021-2024 

The selection of this work is in collaboration with the Arab Documentary Photography Program (ADPP), an initiative that provides support and mentorship to photographers from across the Arab region. 

The Arab Fund for Arts and Culture in partnership with Magnum Foundation and the Prince Claus Fund established the ADPP to stimulate compelling work by Arab Photographers working across a range of experimental styles of storytelling. 

A hand-drawn map evoking a treasure hunt rather than a migratory route accompanies eerie photographs unveiling the atmosphere of a place stuck between two horizon lines: the desert and the ocean. 

80 Miles to Atlantis and Slow Days in the Fortunate Isle tell the story of the migratory relationship between Tarfaya, Morocco and Fuerteventura in the Canary Islands. The series take place in Tarfaya, a small, personal kingdom split into a historically fallen east and a chimerical, illusory west.
